title: After the oven (Bava Metzia 59b)
hookLine: Rabbi Eliezer is shut out after the argument, and the story warns about wounding words

cards: The argument is over. Over a clay oven, the sages have outvoted Rabbi Eliezer, turned away a carob tree, a stream, leaning walls and even a voice from heaven, and declared: it is not in heaven. The majority has won.
The Talmud could close the story there. It doesn't. It turns instead to the one who lost: Rabbi Eliezer, put under a ban, sitting outside the circle he once taught in.
And then it turns to his household, and to one woman who saw what that loss had done.

teach.b: Start with where the story sits. The oven isn't in a chapter about ovens. It sits in a chapter of Bava Metzia about ona'ah, wronging.

The pages around it are about wronging with words. Don't remind someone who has turned their life around of what they used to do. Don't ask a seller the price of something you have no intention of buying.
And the sages say that one who shames another in public, so the color drains from their face, is like one who sheds blood. Then comes the oven.
Then its aftermath, told through Imma Shalom. She was Rabbi Eliezer's wife, and her brother was Rabban Gamliel, the head of the sages who had banned her husband. She knew what her husband carried.

So, the story says, she kept him from falling on his face in the private prayer of supplication, afraid of what his pain might bring down. One day she was distracted, and found him with his face to the ground.
Get up, she said; you've killed my brother. A horn sounded from Rabban Gamliel's house: he had died. How did you know? her husband asked.
She answered with a tradition from her father's house: all the gates may be locked, except the gates for one who has been wronged.
The cry of the one who was hurt goes straight up. That's the warning the page leaves. Winning an argument is allowed; it's how the law moves forward.
But the person on the losing side still has a face, and that gate stays open.

how: The laws against wronging with words (ona'at devarim) are studied as part of Jewish ethics and law, and the story of Rabbi Eliezer and Imma Shalom is often taught alongside them as a warning about how the winners treat the one who lost.

o: what the story tells after the argument is won
the vote that settled the oven's purity law
the rule for cooking on a clay oven on a feast

games.q: who's who after the oven — tap the pairs.
p: her brother, head of the sages

s: the oven story sits in a chapter about wronging people
the pages around it warn about wounding with words.
the Talmud ends the oven story when the sages win
it follows the one who lost, and his household.
Imma Shalom was Rabban Gamliel's sister
her husband was banned by her brother's court.

games.q: you're Imma Shalom. your husband was banned by your brother's court, and he still carries the hurt. what do you do?
o: urge him to cry out against your brother.
keep him from falling on his face in prayer, afraid of what his pain might bring.
games.why: she keeps watch, because she knows the gate for the wronged is never locked. the one day she is distracted, her brother dies.

practice: Bring to mind someone who lost recently, an argument, a vote, a job, a place in the group; maybe you were on the winning side. See their face as it is now, not as it was in the fight, and let their disappointment be real to you.
Then think of one word that would give them back their dignity.

wordCard.voice: After the oven. The part of the story after the argument is won: the one who lost, the hurt he carried, and the gate that stays open for the wronged. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: words wound. Even when the argument was yours to win. Go gently.
